pageData.title: The Study of History & the Rise of Civilizations
pageData.para1:
The Study of History & the Rise of Civilizations. History is the study of the human past through evidence. Historians do not simply memorize dates; they ask how we know what happened, and they test claims against sources. The raw material of history comes in several kinds. Written sources include inscriptions on stone and clay, letters, tax records, law codes, king lists, and chronicles. Material sources come from archaeology: buildings, tools, pottery, weapons, jewelry, and even seeds and bones that reveal what people grew and ate. Oral traditions, such as epics sung for generations before being written down, preserve memory but must be read with care, because they mix real events with legend. A careful historian compares sources against each other.

When an Assyrian king boasts that he destroyed a city, and archaeologists find a burned layer in that city's ruins dated to the right years, the two sources confirm each other. When sources disagree, historians ask who wrote each one, when, and why, because every author had a purpose. To organize the past, historians divide time into periods. Prehistory is the long span before writing; history in the strict sense begins when people start keeping written records, which happened first in Sumer and Egypt around 3200-3000 BC. Events are dated BC (Before Christ) or AD (Anno Domini), and modern scholars often use BCE and CE, which count the same years. Timelines let us see which societies existed at the same time: the pyramids of Giza were already ancient when Abraham lived, and Athens was building the Parthenon while Japan was still in its age of rice-farming villages.
pageData.para2:
A civilization is a complex way of organizing human life, and this course traces four of them: Egypt, Iraq (Mesopotamia), Greece, and Japan. Civilizations share common features, and understanding these features explains why they appeared where they did. The first requirement is a food surplus. When farming produces more grain than farmers themselves eat, some people are freed to become potters, priests, soldiers, scribes, and kings. This is why the earliest civilizations rose along great rivers: the Nile in Egypt, and the Tigris and Euphrates in Iraq, where floodwater made dry land fertile. The second feature is cities, dense settlements where specialization and trade could flourish. The third is government: leaders who organize labor, collect taxes, enforce laws, and lead armies. The fourth is writing, invented first to record grain deliveries and debts, then used for laws, letters, literature, and history itself.

The fifth is organized religion, which explained the world, justified rulers, and bound communities together through shared rituals and temples. Finally come monumental building and specialized art, from pyramids and ziggurats to temples and sculpture, which displayed a society's wealth and beliefs. Civilizations also interact. Mesopotamia and Egypt traded with each other through the Levant; Greece learned writing from the Phoenicians and mathematics from Egypt and Babylon; Japan deliberately imported writing, Buddhism, and government models from China and Korea. No civilization developed in isolation, and no civilization lasts forever: each unit of this course follows its society from rise, through achievement, to decline, and asks what later peoples learned from it. The course also asks why civilizations rise and decline, and the rivers are only the beginning of the answer.

Egypt was protected by deserts and sea, which let one kingdom endure for three thousand years; Iraq's open plain made it rich and invaded in turn by Sumerians, Akkadians, Babylonians, Assyrians, Persians, Greeks, Arabs, and Mongols, so that its history is a story of successive empires; Greece, cut into valleys and islands by mountains, never unified but produced fiercely independent city-states whose rivalry drove both war and creativity; Japan, an island chain protected by the sea yet close enough to learn from China, could choose when to open and when to close, a freedom Egypt and Iraq never had. Geography is not destiny, but it sets the terms on which peoples make their history.

The other great lesson is that civilizations decline from within as much as from without: empires fall when taxes crush the peasants, when elites fight for power, when armies become kingmakers, or when the center can no longer maintain the canals, roads, and trust on which everything rests. Students who learn to see these patterns in Sumer, Egypt, Greece, and Japan are learning to read their own world. Writing itself deserves a place among the marks of civilization, because it changed what humans can remember and therefore what they can build. Before writing, knowledge died with the elders; after it, laws, observations, stories, and accounts accumulated beyond any single memory, and societies could administer kingdoms too large for any king to see.

It is no accident that the first scripts, Sumerian cuneiform and Egyptian hieroglyphs, appeared within centuries of the first cities, or that the earliest texts are mostly lists of grain, labor, and goods: the state was writing's first customer. Only later did writing turn to literature, law, and history, the uses that let civilizations reflect on themselves. Students should also notice what civilization costs: monuments were raised by taxes and labor, cities bred disease and hierarchy, and the freedom of the scribe rested on the toil of the farmer. History honestly told includes both the pyramid and the hands that built it. That double vision, wonder at what humans achieved together and honesty about its price, is the habit this course tries to teach, because a civilization's story, like a student's, is measured not only by its glories but by what it learned.

pageData.title: The Old Kingdom of Egypt
pageData.para1:
The Old Kingdom of Egypt. Around 3100 BC, King Narmer of Upper Egypt united the Two Lands, the Nile Valley in the south and the Delta in the north, into a single kingdom that would endure in some form for three thousand years. After two dynasties of consolidation, the Old Kingdom proper began with the Third Dynasty around 2686 BC, and it is remembered above all as the age of the pyramids. King Djoser's architect Imhotep stacked six mastaba tombs into the Step Pyramid at Saqqara, the first monumental stone building in the world. In the Fourth Dynasty, Sneferu built three pyramids, experimenting with the bent and true forms, and his son Khufu raised the Great Pyramid at Giza: about 2.3 million stone blocks, aligned to the cardinal points with astonishing precision, the tallest human structure for more than 3,800 years.

Khafre and Menkaure added their own pyramids beside it, guarded by the Great Sphinx. These were not tombs built by slaves, as old films suggest: workmen's quarters and overseers' houses excavated at Giza show the work was done by Egyptians, many highly skilled, working for compensation - rotating crews fed and housed in workers' towns, organized by a state that could count, store, and redistribute grain on a vast scale. Royal authority was supported by governors called nomarchs, who administered the provinces or nomes, and by a vizier who ran the bureaucracy. Over time, however, the crown's wealth drained into temple endowments and provincial families. The unusually long reign of Pepi II, perhaps over ninety years in the Sixth Dynasty, ended with an aging court and ambitious local rulers. Around 2181 BC central authority gave way: local governors and the priesthood had grown too strong, a severe drought brought famine the government could not relieve, and the exceptionally long reign of Pepi II left succession uncertain - causes scholars still weigh against one another.

Egypt fragmented into the First Intermediate Period, and the lesson was lasting: Egyptian unity depended on a strong center that could manage the river and the harvest. The unification itself is pictured on the Narmer Palette, where the king wears the crowns of both lands and smites his enemies, an image of kingship that Egyptians would repeat for three thousand years. The central government that emerged assessed the land, levied the harvest, and mobilized tens of thousands for building, and its records in ink on papyrus and stone show an administration counting everything from cattle to work gangs. Pyramid building itself was economic policy as much as religion: much of the workforce was made up of farmers the state could employ when the Nile's flood made farming impossible, fed from its granaries and bound to the crown through common work.

The standard of the age was order: texts boast that the king upheld ma'at against chaos, and the bureaucracy of scribes, with its titles, seals, and archives, ran what one scholar calls a bureaucracy possibly unparalleled in world history for the amount of construction it organized. When that order broke down after Pepi II, the sages who wrote the lamentations of the First Intermediate Period remembered anarchy as the Nile's gift ungiven: the land spun like a potter's wheel, they said, and the poor became rich while the rich begged, an inversion of the sacred order that Egyptians felt in their bones as catastrophe.
pageData.para2:
Old Kingdom society was shaped by the Nile. The river flooded predictably each summer, depositing rich silt; farmers planted wheat and barley as the waters receded and harvested in spring. This dependable cycle created the surplus that fed pyramid builders and priests, and it explains why Egyptians saw the world as fundamentally ordered and good. At the top stood the pharaoh, not merely a king but a living god, the son of Ra and the earthly form of Horus, responsible for maintaining ma'at, the cosmic order of justice, balance, and truth. Below him came viziers, priests, and scribes, whose mastery of hieroglyphic and cursive hieratic writing gave them control of records and therefore of power. Most people were peasant farmers who paid taxes in grain and owed labor service to the state.

Religion permeated everything: Egyptians worshipped many gods, above all the sun god, and believed in an afterlife that the king's pyramid was built to secure. The Pyramid Texts inscribed in the later pyramids are Egypt's earliest surviving substantial religious literature, and the same beliefs drove mummification and the stocking of tombs with food, furniture, and servant statues. Art followed a strict canon: the human figure shown with head and legs in profile, eye and shoulders frontal, proportioned on a grid, built to last for eternity rather than to imitate a fleeting moment. Trade reached south to Nubia for gold, east to Punt for incense, and north to Byblos for Lebanese cedar. Mathematics served surveying and engineering, medicine produced some of the earliest written case studies, and a solar calendar of 365 days, divided into flood, planting, and harvest seasons, organized the year.

The Old Kingdom created the pattern of Egyptian civilization that later ages would look back to as their classical ideal.

pageData.title: The Middle Kingdom of Egypt
pageData.para1:
The Middle Kingdom of Egypt. After a century of division, Egypt was reunified around 2055 BC by Mentuhotep II of Thebes, who defeated his northern rivals and reopened the roads, mines, and trade routes that civil war had closed. His dynasty gave way to the Twelfth Dynasty, founded by Amenemhat I around 1985 BC, who moved the capital to the new planned city of Itjtawy near the Faiyum and, in a strikingly honest text called the Instruction of Amenemhat, warns his son to trust no one, speaking as a king after an attempt on his life. The Twelfth Dynasty ruled Egypt for nearly two centuries, one of the most stable and productive periods in its history.

Sesostris III broke the power of the old provincial nomarch families, reorganized the kingdom's administration, and pushed the southern frontier past the Second Cataract of the Nile into Nubia, where he built a chain of massive mud-brick fortresses such as Buhen and Semna to control the gold trade. His successors turned to the Faiyum depression west of the Nile, where Amenemhat III oversaw a huge land-reclamation project: dikes and canals regulated the lake, and new farmland expanded the kingdom's food supply. Middle Kingdom kings still built pyramids, but now of mud brick with stone casings, smaller and less enduring than those at Giza. After Amenemhat III, a series of short reigns weakened the dynasty, and the Thirteenth Dynasty rotated kings rapidly while central authority slipped away.

Around 1650 BC the Hyksos, a people of western Asian origin who had settled in the Delta and adopted Egyptian customs, seized power in the north, ruling from Avaris with superior military technology: the horse-drawn chariot, the composite bow, and bronze weapons. Egypt split again in the Second Intermediate Period, but the Hyksos occupation would teach Egyptians the new arts of war they needed to build an empire. The reunification was remembered as the work of a second founder, and the Theban kings governed consciously in the shadow of the pyramid age, reviving its styles while correcting its mistakes. Amenemhat I created a professional standing army and, to guard the approaches from Asia, built the Walls of the Ruler in the eastern Delta.

The Nubian fortresses of Sesostris III were a military system complete with signal stations and supply depots, and his boundary stele at Semna forbade Nubians to pass except for trade, an early document of border control. The Faiyum project, with its great lake and canal network, added great tracts of farmland and was remembered in the Greco-Roman age as the work of a king called Moeris. Egypt now projected power abroad as never before: expeditions reopened the Red Sea route to Punt, mining camps worked the copper and turquoise of Sinai, and Egyptian influence reached deep into Syria and Palestine, where rulers paid court to Thebes. The dynasty also managed succession carefully through co-regency, the old king crowning his heir in his lifetime so that power passed without civil war, a hard-won lesson from the chaos that had destroyed the Old Kingdom.
pageData.para2:
The Middle Kingdom is remembered as Egypt's classical age of literature. In Middle Egyptian, the dialect that schoolchildren would copy for a thousand years, writers produced works of real literary ambition. The Tale of Sinuhe follows a courtier who flees Egypt after a royal assassination, makes his fortune in Syria, and longs in old age to return and be buried at home, a meditation on exile and identity. The Eloquent Peasant dramatizes a wronged farmer whose beautiful speeches force officials to grant him justice, reflecting the period's emphasis on ma'at as a duty the powerful owe the weak. The Instruction of King Merikare advises a ruler to govern well because even kings are judged after death. This literature survives because scribal schools copied it for centuries, and it tells us that Middle Kingdom Egyptians were wrestling with questions of justice, loyalty, and mortality. Religion changed profoundly in this era.

Belief in the afterlife, once reserved for the king, was extended to ordinary officials and commoners. Osiris, god of the afterlife, became the hope of everyone, and guidance texts painted inside wooden coffins gave non-royal Egyptians what had once been reserved for kings. Society became somewhat more mobile; a capable scribe or soldier could rise, and Egyptians began to speak of self-made men. Craftsmanship reached extraordinary refinement: the gold jewelry of princesses like Sithathoryunet, with cloisonne inlay of colored stones. Block statues, squatting figures wrapped in cloaks, offered a new sculptural form for tombs and temples. Trade expeditions sailed to Punt for myrrh and incense and to Lebanon for cedar, while forts in Nubia secured gold, ivory, and ebony. The Middle Kingdom proved that Egypt could be reborn after collapse, a pattern of fragmentation and reunification that would repeat through its long history.

pageData.title: The New Kingdom of Egypt
pageData.para1:
The New Kingdom of Egypt. Around 1550 BC, Ahmose I of Thebes drove the Hyksos out of the Delta and pursued them into Canaan, founding the Eighteenth Dynasty and the era of empire. Determined never again to be ruled by foreigners, Egypt's warrior pharaohs pushed outward. Thutmose I campaigned as far as the Euphrates River in Syria. His daughter Hatshepsut then ruled as pharaoh in her own right for about twenty years, presenting herself in statuary with the king's kilt and false beard, building her terraced mortuary temple at Deir el-Bahari, and sending a celebrated trading expedition to the land of Punt, whose ships returned loaded with incense trees, gold, and exotic animals.

Her stepson Thutmose III became Egypt's greatest conqueror: in seventeen campaigns he defeated a coalition of Canaanite kings at Megiddo around 1457 BC, crossed the Euphrates, and organized an empire stretching from Nubia deep into Syria, held together by garrisons, tribute, and the sons of vassal princes raised at the Egyptian court. Under Amenhotep III the empire enjoyed a golden age of wealth and diplomacy, its capital at Thebes glittering with temples. Then came the strangest episode in Egyptian history: Amenhotep IV, renaming himself Akhenaten, suppressed the old gods, closed their temples, and proclaimed one god, the sun disk Aten, building a new capital at Amarna. The experiment collapsed with his death; the boy king Tutankhamun restored the old religion and died young, his nearly intact tomb the most famous archaeological find of the modern age.

In the Nineteenth Dynasty, Ramesses II fought the Hittite Empire at Kadesh around 1274 BC, a battle he claimed as a victory that was probably a draw, and later signed with the Hittites the world's oldest surviving peace treaty. His long reign left colossal monuments including Abu Simbel. Around 1175 BC Ramesses III repelled the Sea Peoples, but the effort exhausted the treasury, strikes hit the royal tomb builders, and the New Kingdom slowly dissolved. The empire was run as a system. In Nubia, a viceroy called the King's Son of Kush governed from fortified temple towns down to the Fourth Cataract, shipping gold north in quantities that filled the temples and palaces. In Asia, Egyptian strategy rested on the loyalty of Canaanite city-kings, bound by oaths, hostages, and gifts, and on the great fortress and granary cities that anchored the military roads.

Diplomacy matched war: the Amarna Letters show the pharaoh exchanging princesses and gold with Babylon, Assyria, and the Hittites, addressed as brothers, in what modern historians call the Club of Great Powers. Akhenaten's revolution failed partly because it neglected this system: while the king worshipped the Aten, vassal letters begged in vain for troops as the empire frayed. The Nineteenth Dynasty restored the balance, and the treaty with the Hittites after Kadesh fixed spheres of influence in terms recognizably modern.

The late New Kingdom also shows how empires die: the cost of wars, the corruption of officials, the strikes of unpaid tomb workers in Year 29 of Ramesses III, and the growing independence of the high priests of Amun, who ended by ruling Thebes as a state within the state, until the Two Lands drifted apart again into the Third Intermediate Period.
pageData.para2:
Empire transformed Egyptian society. Tribute and plunder from Nubian gold mines and Asian vassals poured into the temples of Amun at Karnak and Luxor, until the priesthood of Amun grew powerful enough to rival the crown itself. A new class of professional soldiers rose, rewarded with land, and scribes administered an imperial bureaucracy that corresponded with Babylon, Assyria, and the Hittites in Akkadian cuneiform, the diplomatic language of the age. The Amarna Letters, clay tablets from Pharaoh's archive, preserve this correspondence, including pleading letters from Canaanite princes. Women in Egypt already enjoyed unusual legal standing for the ancient world: they could own property, initiate lawsuits, and make wills, and Hatshepsut showed a woman could even wear the double crown. Burial practice changed too.

Instead of conspicuous pyramids, New Kingdom pharaohs hid their tombs in the Valley of the Kings, deep rock-cut corridors painted with funerary texts such as the Book of the Dead. Art reached new heights, from the graceful realism of Thutmose's sculpture workshops, which produced the famous bust of Nefertiti, to the strange, elongated naturalism of the Amarna style and the intimate scenes of Akhenaten playing with his daughters. We know daily life unusually well because the village of the royal tomb builders, Deir el-Medina, survives with its houses, laundry lists, love songs, legal disputes, and even records of what may be history's first recorded sit-down strike, when workers downed tools over late grain rations under Ramesses III. Religious life grew both grander and more personal: great festivals filled the calendar, and ordinary people prayed directly to the gods for help with sickness and injustice.

The New Kingdom was ancient Egypt at its richest and most powerful, and its decline showed that even the greatest empire depends on solvency, succession, and order at home.

pageData.title: Sumer
pageData.para1:
Sumer. In the southern plain of Iraq, between and below the Tigris and Euphrates rivers, the world's earliest known civilization took shape. The land was flat and dry, but the rivers flooded unpredictably, so survival depended on cooperation: communities that dug and maintained canals could turn the plain into rich farmland. By around 4000 BC villages were growing into towns, and by 3300 BC Uruk had become something entirely new, a true city of perhaps 40,000 people, centered on great temples such as the White Temple raised on its platform. Sumer was never a single kingdom but a patchwork of independent city-states: Uruk, Ur, Lagash, Kish, Umma, Nippur, Eridu, and others, each with its own patron god, its own temple estates, and its own ruler, who styled himself en or lugal and led both war and worship.

During the Early Dynastic period, roughly 2900 to 2350 BC, these cities competed fiercely for land, water, and prestige. The conflict between Lagash and Umma over a border field is recorded across generations of inscriptions, including the Stele of the Vultures, which shows King Eannatum's soldiers marching over their enemies. The Standard of Ur, a mosaic box found in the royal graves there, shows the two sides of city-state life on its two panels: war, with chariots and prisoners, and peace, with banquets, herds, and musicians. Around 2334 BC Sargon of Akkad, a Semitic-speaking ruler from the north, conquered the Sumerian cities one by one and forged the world's first territorial empire, which his grandson Naram-Sin pushed to its height. Akkadian rule lasted about a century and a half before collapsing under pressure from Gutian tribes.

Sumer rose once more in the Third Dynasty of Ur, when Ur-Nammu and his son Shulgi ran a tightly organized bureaucratic state, built the great ziggurat of Ur, and issued law codes. Around 2004 BC Elamites from Iran sacked Ur and carried off its king, and Sumerian political independence ended forever, though its culture outlived it. The archaeology of the plain tells the same story the tablets do. At Eridu, seventeen temples were built one on top of another across three thousand years, one of the oldest sacred sites in the region, showing how the shrine grew into the city. At Uruk, excavators found mass-produced pottery, beveled-rim bowls used to ration grain to workers, proof that the city fed a labor force on an industrial scale.

The royal cemetery of Ur, dug in the 1920s, revealed the wealth and the terror of the city-state: Queen Puabi was buried in gold and lapis with a lyre, a sledge, and the bodies of dozens of attendants who followed their ruler in death. Sumerian kingship was understood as a gift from the gods, lowered from heaven, and it passed from city to city as the gods willed, an idea that let many small states share one civilization while fighting for its leadership. The economy of the temples and palaces organized irrigation on a scale no family could manage, and the word of the ruler who controlled the canals was law because water was life. Sumer also knew political experiment: the assembly of elders, and in Uruk a second assembly of fighting men, appear in the epic debating peace and war, among the earliest recorded popular assemblies.

When Akkadian and later Babylonian kings ruled the land, they came to Sumerian Nippur for the blessing of Enlil, because legitimacy in Iraq remained Sumerian long after Sumer itself was gone.
pageData.para2:
Sumer's greatest invention was writing. It began around 3300 BC as accounting: temple officials pressed tokens and then wedge-shaped marks into clay tablets to record deliveries of barley, beer, oil, and sheep. The cuneiform script, written with a cut reed, gradually gained signs for sounds and ideas, until scribes could record anything: contracts, hymns, proverbs, letters, mathematics, and literature. Learning the script took years in the tablet house, the edubba, and the scribe who mastered it entered a privileged profession. Religion structured every city. Each city belonged to a patron god whose temple was the largest landowner and employer, and the temple's stepped tower, the ziggurat, rose as an artificial mountain dominating the city.

From Sumerian clay comes one of the earliest great works of literature, the Epic of Gilgamesh, in which the king of Uruk seeks eternal life, survives adventures, loses his friend Enkidu, and learns that immortality is not for mortals; its flood story predates and parallels the biblical account retold across later cultures. Sumerians also wrote the earliest known law collections: Urukagina of Lagash boasts of reforms against corrupt officials, and Ur-Nammu's code sets fixed penalties in money for injuries, centuries before Hammurabi. The economy ran on barley and wool; temples organized spinning and weaving on an industrial scale, and traders traveled far because the plain had no metal, stone, or good timber, importing copper from Oman, tin from far to the east, timber from Lebanon. Sumerian mathematics used a base-sixty system, which is why we still divide hours into sixty minutes and circles into 360 degrees.

The wheel and the sailboat are counted Sumerian inventions, and the plow, the potter's wheel, and the school all make some of their earliest known appearances here. Babylon and Assyria inherited Sumerian gods, literature, law, and learning, so that when later Iraqis studied the past, they studied Sumer.

pageData.title: Babylon
pageData.para1:
Babylon. After the fall of Ur around 2004 BC, southern Iraq fragmented among competing Amorite dynasties, and for two centuries no power dominated. The city of Babylon, on the Euphrates where the two rivers run closest together, was just one modest Amorite kingdom among rivals like Larsa, Eshnunna, Mari, and the great northern power of Assyria. Everything changed under Babylon's sixth king, Hammurabi, who reigned from about 1792 to 1750 BC. For three decades he governed patiently, building canals, temples, and alliances, defeating enemies one at a time rather than all at once. Then, in the last fourteen years of his reign, he struck: he defeated his former ally Rim-Sin of Larsa, conquered Mari and destroyed its magnificent palace, humbled Eshnunna, and forced even Assyria to submit, uniting all of Mesopotamia under Babylon for the first time since Ur.

Hammurabi is remembered above all for his law code, nearly three hundred laws carved in cuneiform on a black stone stele topped by a scene of the king receiving authority from Shamash, the sun god and god of justice. The code regulated prices, wages, marriage, inheritance, slavery, medicine, building standards, and agriculture, and it famously scaled punishments by social class: an injury to a noble cost more than the same injury to a commoner. It was not the first law code, but it was the most complete to survive, and its principle that the state publicly declares the law, so that the strong may not oppress the weak, echoes through all later legal history. After Hammurabi his empire slowly shrank, and around 1595 BC the Hittites marched down the Euphrates, sacked Babylon, and withdrew, leaving the Kassites, a people from the Zagros mountains, to rule Babylon for four centuries.

Babylon rose again under Nebuchadnezzar I around 1125 BC, then endured long Assyrian domination until the Chaldean Nabopolassar and his son Nebuchadnezzar II destroyed Assyria, with the Medes, between 616 and 609 BC. Nebuchadnezzar II rebuilt Babylon into a city that awed the ancient world: the blue-glazed Ishtar Gate, the Processional Way, the great ziggurat Etemenanki, and, by later tradition, the Hanging Gardens. His empire fell in 539 BC when Cyrus the Persian entered Babylon without a battle. The reign of Hammurabi is documented not only by his law code but by hundreds of his letters, which show a king managing everything personally: assigning fields, investigating corrupt judges, ordering the repair of canals, and reminding governors that the water must flow. Irrigation was the state's first duty, and the code itself sets penalties for the farmer who neglects his dikes and floods his neighbor's field.

The stele's prologue declares that Hammurabi was chosen by the gods to cause justice to prevail and to destroy the wicked, so that the strong should not oppress the weak, a statement of the purpose of law that still reads as a charter of government. After the Kassite centuries, when Babylon was respected as the ancient holy city even by its foreign rulers, the Assyrian period tested Babylonian identity: the city rebelled again and again, was destroyed by Sennacherib and rebuilt by Esarhaddon, and finally led the coalition that destroyed Assyria itself. Nebuchadnezzar II's rebuilt capital, with walls wide enough, said the Greeks, for chariots to pass on top, was the marvel that travelers like Herodotus described; it was also the city of the Jewish exile, whose prophets and scholars, sitting by the rivers of Babylon, wrote some of the Bible's most famous words.

When Cyrus entered in 539 BC, his cylinder proclaimed in Babylonian tradition that he had come at Marduk's call to restore the sanctuaries and free the captives, and the exiles went home: Babylon had become the measure by which conquerors proved their worth.
pageData.para2:
Babylonian civilization was heir to Sumer and teacher to everyone after. Babylonian scholars studied the Sumerian language the way later students studied Latin, copying the Epic of Gilgamesh and the creation epic Enuma Elish, recited every New Year in honor of the city god Marduk. Religion centered on great temple households, and the temple of the city god Marduk, with its seven-story ziggurat, dominated the capital. Temple scholars kept nightly records of the heavens for centuries, believing the stars held signs, and from this long observation came Babylon's most influential science: astronomy. Its scholars discovered that eclipses and planetary motions repeat in calculable cycles, and invented mathematical astronomy so precise that Greek astronomers later borrowed its methods and data.

The Babylonian base-sixty number system, with place value and an early placeholder for zero, let them solve quadratic equations, calculate compound interest, and produce the tablet known as Plimpton 322, which lists what we now call Pythagorean triples a thousand years before Pythagoras. Our sixty-minute hour and 360-degree circle are Babylonian inheritance. The economy rested on irrigated barley and date palms, managed by temples and palaces but increasingly also by private merchant families like the Egibi, whose surviving archives show them financing trade, farming, and tax collection across generations. Society was stratified into free citizens, a dependent class, and slaves, with law fixing the rights and obligations of each; women could own property, run businesses, and appear in court, especially if they were priestesses or widows.

When Cyrus captured Babylon, he presented himself not as a destroyer but as Marduk's chosen restorer, and the city's temples, scholars, and astronomical diaries continued under Persian, Greek, and Parthian rule, making Babylon one of the intellectual capitals of the ancient world for fifteen hundred years.
